hints: Look carefully at the two curves and the four points. Which curve is high CO2 and which points are low down on the y-axis where saturation with oxygen is very low?
Remember when haemoglobinic acid (HHb) forms: it needs lots of H+ ions from CO2 plus lots of deoxyhaemoglobin ready to pick up those H+ ions.
walkthrough:
**Recall what haemoglobinic acid is**

Think of it simply. In respiring tissues, CO2 forms H+ ions, and deoxyhaemoglobin picks them up to become haemoglobinic acid, HHb.

So you need two things together:
$$CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H^+ + HCO_3^-$$ then $$H^+ + Hb \rightarrow HHb$$

**Work out the two conditions for most HHb**

First, you need high partial pressure of CO2 to make lots of H+ ions. Second, you need low saturation with oxygen, so there is lots of deoxyhaemoglobin (Hb) free to bind H+.

High oxygen saturation means haemoglobin is already full of oxygen, so it cannot form much HHb.

**Apply this to points A, B, C and D**

Points C and D are high up, with high percentage saturation, so very little deoxyhaemoglobin. Points A and B are low down, with low saturation.

Point B is on the dashed high carbon dioxide curve AND at low oxygen saturation. That combination gives the most H+ plus the most Hb, so the highest HHb concentration.

options.A: Point A has low oxygen saturation which is good, but it is on the low CO2 curve, so fewer H+ ions are made to form HHb.
options.B: Point B combines high CO2 (lots of H+ made) with low oxygen saturation (lots of deoxyhaemoglobin), giving the maximum formation of haemoglobinic acid.
options.C: Point C is on the low CO2 curve and at very high oxygen saturation, so there is almost no deoxyhaemoglobin and little H+ to make HHb.
options.D: Point D is on the high CO2 curve, but saturation is very high, so haemoglobin is almost fully oxygenated with little capacity to take up H+.
